151.quote_or_event: “The God-conscious being has a steady patience, like the earth, which is dug up by one, and anointed with sandal paste by another.”
151.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan compares the patience of the God-conscious person to the earth, which stays the same whether it is dug into or honoured with sandalwood.
151.tie_back: The Kural's image is the earth that keeps holding up those who dig into it; Guru Arjan uses the very same image of the dug-up earth for steady forbearance.
151.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 272, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 8, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
151._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: same earth-dug-up image for patience; Gurbani stresses equanimity toward praise and injury alike, while the Kural adds that the earth keeps supporting the digger.

152.quote_or_event: “So erase your duality and hold tight to forgiveness,”
152.explanation: Bhagat Kabir tells the seeker to give up the divided, restless mind and hold firmly to forgiveness.
152.tie_back: The Kural asks us to bear even extreme wrongs and better still to forget them; Kabir likewise asks for a forgiveness held fast, not grudgingly.
152.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 343, Raag Gauri, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
152._accuracy_note: Next-best: shares the call to forgiveness, but lacks the Kural's two-step from bearing a wrong to forgetting it entirely.

153.quote_or_event: “if you are powerful, be weak; … How rare is one who is known as such a devotee.”
153.explanation: A salok in the Guru Granth Sahib describes the rare devotee who, though strong, lives as if powerless; the same salok also praises sharing with others even when one has little.
153.tie_back: The Kural calls bearing with fools the strength within strength and failing a guest the poverty within poverty; this salok joins strength held back with generosity in the same way.
153.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, Salok 128 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
153._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on restrained strength paired with giving; the salok does not mention fools or guests explicitly, and the sharing line is paraphrased, not quoted.

154.quote_or_event: “Let patience be your purpose in life; implant this within your being. In this way, you will grow into a great river; you will not break off into a tiny stream.”
154.explanation: Sheikh Farid says that patience made firm within turns a person into a great river instead of a broken trickle.
154.tie_back: The Kural says patience is what keeps one's fullness of character from being lost; Farid's image of the river that grows rather than breaks off makes the same point.
154.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, Salok 117 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
154._accuracy_note: Strong fit: patience as what preserves and enlarges one's wholeness; the Kural's term nirai (self-possession, integrity) is broader than the river image.

155.quote_or_event: “When something is placed on the balancing scale and weighed, the side which descends is heavier.”
155.explanation: Guru Nanak uses the scale to show that the one who bows low is found to weigh more.
155.tie_back: The Kural says people count the punisher as nothing and treasure the forbearing like wrapped gold; Guru Nanak likewise says the one who yields proves the more valuable when weighed.
155.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
155._accuracy_note: Partial: the verse praises humility in general rather than refusing to retaliate, though both reverse the honour given to the one who strikes back.

156.quote_or_event: Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, is remembered as Sikhism's first martyr: ordered by the emperor Jahangir to remove supposedly offensive passages from the Adi Granth, he refused and was tortured to death at Lahore in 1606.
156.explanation: Sikhs honour Guru Arjan's endurance of torture without yielding as one of the defining moments of their history.
156.tie_back: The Kural says the pleasure of revenge lasts a day while the fame of the forbearing lasts as long as the world; the Guru's endured suffering has won him lasting honour among Sikhs.
156.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Guru Arjan' (Tamanna Nangia, fact-checked by Britannica Editors)
156._accuracy_note: Next-best: endurance winning lasting renown fits, but the event concerns refusing to alter scripture rather than declining personal revenge, and the Kural's pleasure-of-revenge contrast is absent.

157.quote_or_event: “Fareed, do not turn around and strike those who strike you with their fists. Kiss their feet, and return to your own home.”
157.explanation: Sheikh Farid teaches not to hit back at those who hurt us, but to answer them with humility and go home at peace.
157.tie_back: The Kural says that even when wronged without cause one should not do anything unrighteous in return; Farid gives the same counsel in concrete form.
157.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, Salok 7 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
157._accuracy_note: Strong fit on refusing to retaliate; the Kural's added note of grieving for the suffering the wrongdoer will bring on himself is not present.

158.quote_or_event: “Humility is my spiked club. … No evil-doer can withstand these weapons.”
158.explanation: Guru Arjan describes humility as a weapon before which no wrongdoer can stand.
158.tie_back: The Kural tells us to conquer the arrogant by our own worth, that is, by patience, and uses the language of victory; Guru Arjan likewise turns humility into a weapon that defeats the evil-doer.
158.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 628, Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
158._accuracy_note: Strong fit on non-retaliation as a form of victory, in martial terms; humility (garibi) is close to but not identical with the Kural's patience.

159.quote_or_event: “Those who are patient abide in patience; in this way, they burn their bodies. They are close to the Lord, but they do not reveal their secret to anyone.”
159.explanation: Sheikh Farid says the patient make patience itself their austerity, and so come close to God.
159.tie_back: The Kural says those who bear insults from transgressors are as pure as renunciants; Farid likewise treats patience as an inner austerity that brings one near the divine.
159.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, Salok 116 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
159._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on patience as tapas; the salok does not mention bearing harsh words, and its Sikh setting favours the householder over the renunciant the Kural uses as a benchmark.

160.quote_or_event: “To practice forgiveness is the true fast, good conduct and contentment.”
160.explanation: Guru Nanak redefines fasting: the real vow is forgiveness, together with good conduct and contentment.
160.tie_back: The Kural ranks those who fast below those who endure cruel words; Guru Nanak likewise puts forbearance in the place of the outward fast.
160.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 223, Raag Gauri, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
160._accuracy_note: Strong fit on ranking forbearance above literal fasting, which Sikh teaching does not prescribe; the verse speaks of forgiveness generally rather than of enduring insult, and it is also used for Kural 130.
